records.t: Agentic observability: what leaders should require before agents reach production
records.x: Agents turn one request into a tree of decisions, model calls and tool calls. The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions give that tree a shared vocabulary. Eight requirements to adopt.

s.t: Agents are distributed systems that make decisions
s.x: A conventional service does what its code says. An agent decides what to do next. A single customer request might cause an orchestrator to start two agents; one of them plans, calls a model, calls a policy-lookup tool through an MCP server, calls the model again, and hands off. The other retries a slow database call before it answers. None of that sequence existed before the request arrived, and the next request will produce a different one. That has three consequences for anyone accountable for the program: Cost is emergent. It depends on how many model calls and tool calls the agent chose to make, not on a fixed per-request price. Failure is partial. An agent can return a confident answer after a tool call silently failed. Nothing errors and nothing alerts, yet the output is wrong. Accountability needs a record. When an agent takes an action on a customer's behalf, someone will ask what it saw, what it decided and which systems it touched. The answer to all three is the same engineering artifact: a trace. A trace records the run as a tree of timed operations, which are called spans, each with a name and attributes. Distributed tracing is mature for ordinary services. What was missing for agents was an agreed way to name the spans and attributes, so that traces from different frameworks, vendors and teams mean the same thing.

The OpenTelemetry project maintains semantic conventions for generative AI. They define, for any GenAI system: Spans for model operations (chat, text completion, embeddings, retrieval, memory) and for agent operations: creating an agent, invoking an agent, invoking a workflow, planning, and executing a tool. Metrics for operation duration, agent and workflow duration, tool duration, the number of model and tool calls per agent invocation, and token usage including cached and reasoning tokens. Events for evaluation results and for exceptions. Protocol coverage for the Model Context Protocol, including how trace context crosses from an MCP client into an MCP server. Provider mappings for Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Inference and OpenAI. The strategic value is not any single attribute. It is that a framework, a model vendor, an MCP server and your own platform can all emit telemetry that lands in the same backend and joins into one tree. That is what turns observability from a per-team project into a program-wide capability, and it is what keeps you from being locked in to one vendor's console. Every document in the set is marked Development. Names and requirement levels can still change. Section 6 covers how to adopt now without being caught out later.

s.t: What one agent run looks like
s.x: The exhibit below is a single run of a hypothetical claims-triage workflow, drawn the way a tracing tool would show it. Each row is a span. Indentation is the parent–child relationship and the bar is when the span ran. span name 0 s 4.2 s 8.4 s duration invoke_workflow claims-triage 8.40 s invoke_agent intake-agent 2.80 s plan intake-agent 0.73 s chat example-model-large 0.69 s execute_tool lookup_policy 0.60 s chat example-model-large 1.25 s invoke_agent fraud-check-agent 5.30 s chat example-model-small 0.65 s execute_tool query_ledger error.type = timeout 3.00 s execute_tool query_ledger 0.60 s chat example-model-small 0.80 s workflow agent / plan model inference tool execution error Exhibit 1. Illustrative trace of one agent run. Synthetic data: the workflow, agents, tools and model names are invented. Span names follow the conventions: invoke_workflow {gen_ai.workflow.name}, invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}, plan {gen_ai.agent.name}, {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model} and execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}. Read top to bottom, the trace tells the story a leader needs. One workflow ran two agents. The intake agent planned and then looked up a policy. The fraud check spent more than a third of the whole run waiting on a ledger query that timed out and was retried. Every model call carries the tokens it consumed, so the cost of this run can be added up span by span and charged to the workflow and the agents responsible. A few conventions make this tree trustworthy across teams: Remote and in-process agents are distinguished. An agent invoked over a remote service (the conventions cite OpenAI Assistants and AWS Bedrock Agents) is a CLIENT span. An agent running inside your process (LangChain or CrewAI, for example) is an INTERNAL span. Workflows are reported only at real entry points. invoke_workflow is for user-facing orchestrations that coordinate several agents or GenAI calls, not for a runner that a framework starts behind the scenes. Planning is reported only when it can be identified reliably. A plan span marks the phase where an agent decides its strategy. The model call that produces the plan is its child, and the work that follows sits beside it under the agent. MCP calls join the same trace. Instrumentations propagate trace context inside the MCP request's params._meta, so a tool server owned by another team appears in your tree. Where an outer GenAI instrumentation already traces the tool call, MCP adds its attributes to that span instead of creating a duplicate.

Executives do not need to learn attribute names, but they should know that each of their recurring questions has a specific, standard answer. If your platform team cannot produce these, the gap is in instrumentation, not in reporting. The question The standard signal What does a completed task cost, and which agent spent it? Token counts on each inference span, including cached and reasoning tokens, rolled up through the trace to the agent and workflow. gen_ai.usage.input_tokens gen_ai.usage.output_tokens gen_ai.client.inference.usage.reasoning.output_tokens Is an agent doing more work than it should? Distributions of model calls and tool calls per agent invocation. A long tail usually means loops, retries or a bad prompt. gen_ai.invoke_agent.inference_calls gen_ai.invoke_agent.tool_calls Where does the time go? Durations at every level, from the whole workflow down to time to first token from the model server. gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration gen_ai.execute_tool.duration gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token Was the answer any good? An evaluation event attached to the span it judges, with a named metric, a score and an explanation. gen_ai.evaluation.result gen_ai.evaluation.score.value gen_ai.evaluation.score.label What failed, and did the user notice? Span status and a low-cardinality error type on the failing span, plus an exception event for client-side failures such as rate limits and timeouts. error.type gen_ai.client.operation.exception Which agent, which version, which conversation, which model? Stable identity on every agent span, the provider, and the model requested versus the model that actually answered. gen_ai.agent.name gen_ai.agent.version gen_ai.conversation.id gen_ai.provider.name gen_ai.response.model What did it touch? A span for every tool execution, including tools reached through MCP and agent skills, with the tool's name and type. gen_ai.tool.name gen_ai.tool.type gen_ai.skill.name

s.t: Content capture is a governance decision
s.x: The most consequential setting in agent telemetry is whether to record content: the system instructions, the messages sent to the model, the model's output, tool definitions, tool-call arguments and results, retrieval queries and memory records. The conventions treat all of these as Opt-In attributes, and they warn that message content is likely to include sensitive information, including personal data. Engineers will reasonably want content turned on, because it makes debugging far easier. Legal, privacy and security functions will reasonably want it off. The conventions give you both paths. You can keep content out of telemetry, capture it under explicit configuration, or send it to separate storage through an upload hook that is independent of the capture flags. Which path each environment takes is a policy choice with an owner. It should not be a default someone accepted in a pull request.

These are written so that they can be copied into a platform standard, a program charter or a vendor contract. Each one links to the section above that motivates it and to the source in the conventions. The key words MUST, MUST NOT and SHOULD are to be read as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 when, and only when, they appear in capitals. R1 AI programs MUST emit agent and model telemetry using the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. Contracts for agent platforms, frameworks and model gateways MUST require it, and MUST NOT accept telemetry available only in a vendor's own console. § 2 · R2 Every user-facing agent entry point MUST produce a single connected trace from workflow to individual tool call, including across MCP servers operated by other teams. § 3 · · R3 Every agent in production MUST report a stable name and version, so that cost, quality and incidents can be attributed to a specific agent and a specific release. § 4 · R4 Cost reporting MUST be derived from token usage on inference spans, including cached and reasoning tokens, and MUST be attributable per agent and per workflow rather than only per API key or account. § 4 · R5 Programs SHOULD alert on the distribution of model calls and tool calls per agent invocation, not only on latency and error rate, so that runaway loops are detected before they appear on an invoice. § 4 · R6 Quality SHOULD be measured with evaluation events attached to the spans they judge, using named evaluation metrics that are reviewed with the business owner of the workflow. § 4 · R7 Capture of prompts, outputs, system instructions and tool arguments MUST be disabled unless a written policy enables it for a named environment, with an accountable owner, a retention period and access controls. § 5 · R8 Because the conventions are in Development status, programs MUST record which version of the conventions each service emits and SHOULD plan upgrades as normal platform work, so that dashboards and cost reports do not break when names change. § 2 ·

Days 1–30: one workflow, end to end. Choose the agent workflow closest to production that has a real business owner. Instrument it with the conventions, keep content capture off, and confirm that a single request produces one connected trace that includes the tool calls (R2, R3, R7). Days 31–60: the four numbers. Publish cost per completed task, the distribution of model and tool calls per invocation, tool error rate, and end-to-end duration for that workflow. Add one evaluation metric agreed with the business owner (R4, R5, R6). Days 61–90: make it the standard. Write R1 to R8 into the platform standard and procurement templates, pin the convention version, and review a handful of real traces with the leadership team. Looking at traces together builds a shared, concrete sense of how the agents actually behave faster than any summary dashboard.

Being specific about maturity is part of the guidance: All of the GenAI conventions are in Development status, so names, requirement levels and span structure can change. Events, which carry evaluation results and exceptions, are not yet available in every OpenTelemetry language SDK. Structured content attributes may need to be serialized to JSON on spans in some languages until complex attribute values are supported everywhere. Coverage depends on each framework's instrumentation. For example, planning spans appear only where an instrumentation can tell planning apart from an ordinary model call. None of this is a reason to wait. The cost of instrumenting against a moving standard is a planned upgrade. The cost of running agents without a shared trace is finding out what they did only after a customer, an auditor or an invoice tells you.

records.t: Test triangulation: properties that say what must never happen
records.x: Example tests check only the cases an engineer thought of. Triangulate: state the properties that constrain the behaviour, including what must never happen, and let a framework try thousands of inputs to find a counterexample. Then map the value stream to see where late defects cost time.

s.x: Most test suites are a list of examples. An engineer picks an input, works out the expected output and asserts it. That is useful, and it has a ceiling: the suite checks the cases somebody thought of. Aniche starts from the same limit. Exhaustive testing is impossible, so testing is a matter of choosing inputs well and knowing when to stop. In his words, “No matter what testing you do, it will never be perfect or enough”. Coding agents make the ceiling lower. An agent can write a feature and its tests in the same minute. If both come from the same reading of the requirement, they share its blind spots: a misread rule produces code and tests that agree with each other and are both wrong. Reviewers cannot read every line any more, so the suite has to find the cases nobody looked for. Triangulation is borrowed from surveying, where a point is fixed by taking bearings from more than one place. In testing it means checking one behaviour from several independent angles, so that a gap one angle misses is caught by another.

Effective Software Testing builds a developer's suite in layers. It starts from the specification, adds tests the source code reveals, designs contracts into the code, and then states properties for a framework to check. Each layer finds something the others miss. The angle What it finds, and what it misses Examples from the specification Finds wrong outputs for the partitions and boundaries read from the requirement. Misses partitions nobody noticed when reading it. Structural coverage of the code Finds branches and conditions no test exercises. In Aniche's words, “you may have forgotten a partition or two when analyzing the requirements”. Misses behaviour the code does not implement at all. Coverage shows which lines ran, not that they were right. Contracts in the code Finds broken pre-conditions, post-conditions and invariants at the moment they break, in tests and in production. Misses inputs that never reach the contract. Properties checked by a framework Finds counterexamples to a stated rule across thousands of generated inputs, including combinations nobody would write by hand. Misses rules nobody wrote down, and inputs the generator cannot produce. No single angle is enough. The useful signal is disagreement: a branch that no specification test reaches, or a property that fails on an input the examples skipped, marks a gap in the code or in the understanding of the requirement. Of the four, properties change the most about how tests are written, so the rest of this note concentrates on them.

An example-based test encodes one engineer's idea of a case: charge 120, refund 30, expect 90 left. The engineer chooses the input, so the test inherits the engineer's assumptions about which inputs matter. Property-based testing takes that choice away. Aniche describes the shift directly: “We do not pick a concrete example; rather, we define a property (or a set of properties) that the program should adhere to, and the test framework tries to find a counterexample.” The engineer's job changes from choosing inputs to stating constraints. A property is a rule that must hold for every valid input. The output of a sort is in order and contains the same elements as the input. A discount never takes a price below zero. Serialising a message and parsing it again returns the original. Together, the properties form the constraint set: the team's written claim about what the behaviour is, independent of any particular example. The framework then plays the adversary. It generates inputs, mixes in edge cases such as zero, empty lists and the largest allowed values, and tries to break each property. The test passes only when the framework fails to find a counterexample. When it succeeds, the failing input is evidence that the code, the property or the constraint set is wrong. Examples do not disappear. They remain the clearest way to document a specific case, and every counterexample the framework finds should become one (R5). Aniche compares the two styles and uses both. What changes is that examples are no longer the only description of what the system must do.

s.t: Write down what must never happen
s.x: The most valuable properties are often negative. A system that moves money, grants access or spends a budget is defined as much by what it must never do as by what it does. Writing those rules down is design work, not a testing chore, which is why this note sits at Design on the route. In an AI system, the never-rules usually live in the ordinary code around the model: A refund never exceeds the amount charged. An agent never calls a tool outside the permissions of the user it acts for. Retries for one request never exceed their budget, however the failures are arranged. Retries without a budget are on Hold on the radar as unbudgeted automatic retries. A parser never passes on model output that fails its schema. Rules like these are what the radar calls controls enforced outside the model. That code is deterministic, so a generated input either breaks the rule or it does not, and properties are the most direct way to test it. Many never-rules are also invariants in Aniche's sense, so the same rule can be enforced as a contract in the code and checked as a property in the tests.

Exhibit 1 is a property for the first rule above, written for jqwik, the Java property-based testing library used in the book. The guard under test checks each refund request against the amount charged. The property does not list cases. It says that, for any charge and any short sequence of requests, the total refunded never exceeds the charge. The property @Property(tries = 10_000) void refundsNeverExceedTheCharge(@ForAll @IntRange(min = 1, max = 100_000) int chargedCents, @ForAll @Size(max = 5) List<@IntRange(min = 1, max = 100_000) Integer> requestsCents) { RefundGuard guard = new RefundGuard(chargedCents); int refundedCents = 0; for (int request: requestsCents) { if (guard.allow(request)) { refundedCents += request; } } assertThat(refundedCents).isLessThanOrEqualTo(chargedCents); } The failure report, abridged tries = 4 | # of calls to property checks = 4 | # of not rejected calls seed = -1428803127462810357 | random seed to reproduce generated values Shrunk Sample (9 steps) ----------------------- chargedCents: 1 requestsCents: [1, 1] Original Sample --------------- chargedCents: 61428 requestsCents: [48310, 27795, 1] Exhibit 1. Illustrative property and failure report. The refund guard, its rule and every number in the report are invented. The report layout follows jqwik's failure reporting, shortened to the lines discussed here. Three things in that report matter to a leader, not only to an engineer: Nobody chose the inputs. jqwik tries each property 1,000 times by default, and the team can raise that, as here, to 10,000. Across a suite of properties, every push runs thousands of test cases that nobody had to write. The counterexample is minimal. After a failure, the framework shrinks the input to the smallest one that still fails: a one-cent charge and two one-cent requests. Nobody has to debug the original 61,428-cent case. The failure is reproducible. The report records the seed, and by default the next run tries the failing sample first, so the failure cannot quietly disappear on the next build.

s.t: A counterexample is a question about the constraint set
s.x: The guard in Exhibit 1 does exactly what its rule says: it rejects any single refund larger than the charge. The property still fails, because two refunds of one cent add up to more than a one-cent charge. In an agent system that input is not exotic. An agent that times out and retries the same refund produces it. Asking why the property failed has three possible answers, and each has a different owner: The code is wrong. The rule meant a limit on the total, and the guard checks each refund on its own. Engineering fixes the guard. The property is wrong. The business allows refunds above the charge, for example as goodwill credits. Engineering corrects the property and records why. The constraint set has a gap. The requirement never said whether the limit applies to each refund or to the total, or whether a retried request counts as a new refund. Neither the engineer nor the agent should guess. The question goes to the owner of the requirement. The third answer is the main reason to do this. A set of properties is a precise statement of what the team believes the rules are. When the framework breaks one, it often shows that the rules were incomplete or contradicted each other. Finding that in a test run costs a conversation; finding it in production costs a dispute with a customer. Tracing each property to the need it protects, in the way Problem-Based SRS traces requirements to customer problems, makes it clear who owns the answer.

s.t: Map the value stream to find the waste
s.x: Section 6 claims that a gap found in a test run costs less than one found later. A value stream map shows how much less, for a particular team. The idea comes from lean thinking, which Mary and Tom Poppendieck applied to software in Lean Software Development. They define waste as “anything that does not add value to a product, value as perceived by the customer”, and give handoffs as an example: “In product development, handing off development from one group to another is waste”. Their first chapter pairs two tools: seeing waste, whose list includes waiting and defects, and value stream mapping. A map follows one request from the moment it is asked for to the moment it is delivered, and records where the time went: doing the work, waiting for it, or doing it again. step day 0 day 10 day 20 duration Write the requirement 0.5 days Wait for a development slot 3 days Agent writes the code and example tests 0.5 days Wait for review 2 days Code review 0.5 days Wait for a test environment 4 days Manual testing finds a double refund 1 day Wait for the requirement owner's answer 3 days Rework, review and test again 1.5 days Wait for the release window 4 days work waiting in a queue defect and rework Exhibit 2. Illustrative value stream map of one change to the refund rule from section 6, from request to release over 20 working days. Synthetic data: the steps, the queues and every duration are invented. A filled bar is work, an outlined bar is time spent waiting in a queue, and red marks the defect and the rework it caused. Read as a value stream, the change was worked on for 4 of its 20 days and waited in a queue for the other 16. Three points of improvement stand out: Faster coding barely moves the total. The agent's half day is already one of the shortest steps on the map; halving it again saves a quarter of a day in twenty. The Poppendiecks observe that experts “have a tendency to maximize the performance of the part of the product representing their own specialty rather than focusing on overall system performance”. Buying faster code generation without looking at the queues makes the same mistake at the scale of a program. Their chapter 7, See the Whole, returns to the theme. The defect was found late, after two handoffs. The code that allowed a double refund was written on day 4 and the defect was found seven working days later, after the change had passed from the agent to a reviewer and from the reviewer to a tester. A property run on every push (R2) fails within minutes of the code being written, before the first queue. The real question was asked last. The defect raised the constraint-set question from section 6: does the limit apply to each refund or to the total? Answering it cost three days of waiting for the requirement owner and a day and a half of rework. Asked on day 0, while the never-list is written with that owner (R1), the same question costs one conversation. In the terms of this note, the map is one more angle. The test suite says whether the code is right; the map says when the team finds out, and what the delay costs. None of the three points is visible from inside a single step: the agent, the reviewer and the tester can each be quick while the change still takes four weeks. The Poppendiecks put the remedy plainly: “Compressing the value stream as much as possible is a fundamental lean strategy for eliminating waste”. Properties compress one part of it by moving the discovery of defects and gaps to the start. Mapping a comparable change again after adopting them (R7) shows whether they did, and where the largest waste now sits.

These are written so that they can be copied into an engineering standard or a definition of done. Each one links to the section above that motivates it. The key words MUST, MUST NOT and SHOULD are to be read as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 when, and only when, they appear in capitals. R1 Every component that enforces a business rule, a permission or a limit MUST have a written list of what must never happen, owned by the person accountable for the rule. § 4 · R2 Each item on that list SHOULD be expressed as a property and run on every push, with the number of tries and the seed recorded in the test report. § 3 · § 5 · R3 Test suites for such components MUST combine more than one angle from section 2. Code coverage alone MUST NOT be accepted as evidence that a component is tested. § 2 · R4 Every counterexample MUST be triaged as a code defect, a wrong property or a gap in the constraint set. Gaps MUST go to the owner of the requirement and MUST NOT be settled by the engineer or agent that found them. § 6 R5 Each shrunk counterexample SHOULD be kept as a named example test, so that the case stays covered when generators or seeds change. § 3 · § 5 R6 Where a coding agent writes the code, properties SHOULD be derived from the requirement separately from that code, by a person or by an agent that has not seen the implementation. § 1 · § 3 R7 Before adopting these requirements, a team SHOULD map at least one change from request to release, recording working time, waiting time and where each defect was found. It SHOULD map a comparable change again afterwards and compare the two. § 7 ·

Map one change, then pick one rule. Follow a recent change from request to release and note where it waited and where its defects were found (R7). Then pick one rule that costs money when it breaks, such as refunds, credits, permission checks or retry budgets, and write its never-list with the rule's business owner (R1). Turn the list into properties. Add a property-based testing library for the team's language; the book's examples use jqwik for Java. Run the properties on every push and keep every shrunk counterexample as an example test (R2, R5). Triage together, then map again. Review the first counterexamples with the business owner and sort each into the three answers from section 6. Map a comparable change and compare it with the first map. Then write R1 to R7 into the definition of done for components that enforce rules (R3, R4, R6).

Being specific about the limits is part of the guidance: Good properties take creativity and practice. Aniche gives a section of the chapter to exactly that, and another to common issues. A property that repeats the implementation proves nothing. If the test computes the expected answer the same way the code does, both carry the same mistake. Generators can be biased. A generator that never produces an empty list, or only produces values in a narrow range, cannot find defects outside it. Passing is not proof. A property that survives 10,000 tries has not found a counterexample in those tries. It has not shown that none exists. Model outputs are not deterministic. Properties test the code around the model. Judging the model's own answers needs repeated trials and evaluation, such as repeated-trial reliability on the radar. One map is an anecdote. A single change can be unusual, and durations recalled from memory can be wrong. Map several changes, taking the times from the tracker and the delivery pipeline where possible, before deciding where the largest waste is. None of this argues for fewer example tests. It argues against letting examples be the only statement of what the system must do.

records.t: Start from the problem, not the model.
records.x: A model can't fix a problem nobody wrote down. I start with who has the problem, what it costs them and how we'll know it's solved. Then every feature has to trace back to it. Agents make this matter more, because they will happily build what nobody asked for.

records.t: Evaluations are the spec you can run.
records.x: I don't trust a prompt, skill or model change I can't test. Deterministic checks run on every push. A model grading outputs earns trust only after it agrees with people grading the same ones. A benchmark score says a model managed someone else's task once, not that my system will, every time.

records.t: If I can't see what an agent did, I can't own it.
records.x: One request to an agent becomes a tree of decisions, model calls and tool calls that nobody wrote down in advance. I want that whole tree as one connected trace, in an open format, before the agent reaches production. Cost, quality and risk all come out of the same record.

records.t: Put the controls outside the model.
records.x: A prompt is not a permission. Each agent gets its own identity and only the access it needs. Limits on spend and loops live in the platform, not in the instructions. People stop reading approval prompts long before an agent stops sending them, so approval can't be the only safeguard. The team that ships it stays accountable.

records.t: Coding agents move the bottleneck. They don't remove it.
records.x: With coding agents, writing code stops being the slow part. Deciding what to build and reviewing what comes back become the work. That makes written intent, small branches and fast checks worth more than before. It's the same discipline that keeps a team spread across time zones moving: write the decision down clearly enough that nobody has to be in the room.

records.t: Tests that state what must never happen
records.x: I'm trying property-based tests on the code around agents: refund limits, permissions, retry budgets. Instead of picking examples, I state what must never happen and let the framework try thousands of inputs to break it. What I'm watching for are failures that point to a rule nobody pinned down.

records.t: A skill that makes the agent trace every feature to a problem
records.x: I'm testing whether an agent skill can keep a coding agent honest about why it builds something. Problem-Based SRS walks it from customer problems to needs to requirements and checks that nothing is left without a parent. It's open source under MIT, for GitHub Copilot and Claude Code.

records.t: Evals on every push, for prompts and skills
records.x: Every push to the Problem-Based SRS repository runs plugin validation, unit tests, deterministic skill evals and a visual suite, then publishes a Skills Health dashboard. I want a prompt change that breaks a skill to fail the same way a code change that breaks the build does.

records.t: Several coding agents, one site, separate branches
records.x: This site was built by coding-agent sessions running in parallel: one curating sources, one on design directions, one on the radar, each on its own branch. What I'm watching is where the sessions drift apart, and how much of the work turns into review.

records.t: One open trace format for agents
records.x: I put the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions in Trial, not Adopt. They name every part of an agent run, from workflow to tool call, but every document is still marked Development. GN-0001 sets out what I'd require now, including pinning the version so renames don't break dashboards.

Give a coding agent a feature request and it builds the feature. Give it the problem and who has it, and its output has something to be checked against. Without that, it fills the gap with plausible features. Naming the problem is the cheapest fix for agent output I know.

Most tasks I'd hand to an agent work better as a fixed workflow with one or two model calls. I reach for an open-ended agent loop only when the steps can't be known in advance, and then with a budget on calls.

Before any model work I want a simple baseline on real data: a rule, a lookup, a heuristic. If the model can't beat it, we stop early. If it can, we know by how much, and the failures get written down, not only the average.

records.t: Cost per completed task, not per call
records.x: I look at cost and at the number of model and tool calls per completed task. An agent that retries its way to an answer looks cheap per call and expensive per task. The GenAI conventions carry the token counts to do this per agent.

records.t: Small branches and checks that run in seconds
records.x: Coding agents produce more change than anyone can review carefully in one sitting. So keep their work on short branches, one concern each, behind checks that run in seconds. On this site that is a zero-dependency build and a link checker that refuses broken anchors.

records.t: Telemetry that lives only in a vendor's console
records.x: If the only place to see what your agents did is one vendor's dashboard, you can't join it to the rest of your traces, and you can't leave. Put it in the contract: open conventions, exported to a backend you control.

A model grading another model's output is cheap and fast, and it can be wrong in ways that look confident. Before a judge gates anything, check it against people grading the same samples, and check again when prompts or models change.

A leaderboard result says a model did well on someone else's tasks, once. It says little about your data, your tools or repeated runs. Launch on results from your own tasks, run several times, with the failures written down.

Automatic retries feel like resilience until a slow dependency turns every request into several, and the overload spreads. Retries need a budget, backoff and a stop, enforced by the platform rather than left to each agent.

records.t: Capturing prompts and outputs by default
records.x: Prompts, outputs and tool arguments often carry personal data. Capturing them makes debugging easier and turns your telemetry into a sensitive data store. Keep capture off unless a written policy turns it on for a named environment, with an owner and a retention period.

records.t: A person approving every step as the only safeguard
records.x: Approval prompts feel safe, but people stop reading them long before the agent stops asking. Keep approval for the decisions that need judgement, and enforce the rest with permissions, limits and checks outside the model.

When an agent gets it wrong, "the model did it" is not an answer. A Canadian tribunal held an airline responsible for what its chatbot told a customer. Whoever deploys the system owns what it says and does, so name that owner before launch.
Measure a simple non-ML or single-call baseline first, and require any model or agent to beat it on the same task, metric and cost.
Use the simplest design that works: a fixed workflow where steps are known, and open-ended agent control only where the task demonstrably needs it.

records.t: Canary releases for model and prompt changes
records.x: Expose each model, prompt or configuration change to a small share of traffic against a control, with quality, latency and cost thresholds agreed before rollout.
Treat quality regressions, harmful outputs and agents acting out of scope as incidents, with written, blameless reviews that end in owned fixes and new evaluations.
Derive requirements from named customer problems through customer needs, so every AI capability traces to a problem it solves and unneeded requirements are cut.
Before scaling, draw the loops where a system's outputs return as its inputs, such as models trained on their own results, and name each delay and limit.
Send each request to the cheapest model that meets the quality bar and escalate only when needed; one study matched the best single model at up to 98% lower cost.
Constrain what an agent can do after reading untrusted content, for example plan-then-execute. The patterns give provable resistance to prompt injection at an explicit cost in utility.
Splitting work across cooperating agents adds documented failure modes in system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. Test against a single agent or workflow before committing.
Agents and clients that retry without limits turn a slow dependency into overload. Cap retries with budgets and jittered backoff, and propagate deadlines through every step.

records.t: W3C Trace Context across agent hops
records.x: Propagate one trace identifier through every agent, tool call, MCP server and queue, so a single request can be reconstructed end to end.

records.t: OAuth to the current security BCP
records.x: Delegate agent access through OAuth as RFC 9700 recommends: audience-restricted, sender-constrained tokens. MCP authorization builds on OAuth, so the same baseline applies.
The open vocabulary for model, agent and tool telemetry. Instrument now, but every document is still in Development status: pin and record the version each service emits.
One open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data, now under Linux Foundation governance. Revisions still change: pin one and review its authorization section.
Keep evaluations as versioned code in an open harness, so the same suite reruns unchanged on every model, prompt or vendor change and results stay comparable.
An open protocol for agents from different teams or vendors to discover each other and delegate tasks. Version 1.0 was released in March 2026; assess it where agents cross organisations.

records.t: Telemetry only in a vendor's console
records.x: Agent telemetry that cannot be exported in open formats leaves traces split by vendor and ties cost and quality reporting to one tool. GN-0001 requires open conventions instead.
Offline evaluations missed production regressions in two public postmortems. Run quality evaluations continuously against live endpoints, and add each incident's failure as a new test.
Report every evaluation result with its cost per task. Accuracy alone has led to needlessly complex, costly agents and to wrong conclusions about what drives gains.
Track p99 latency for each model and tool call and for the whole run. Rare slow calls come to dominate performance as agents chain more steps.
Treat a measurement as reducing uncertainty for a named decision. Use the value of information to decide what to measure, including benefits called intangible.
Give each AI feature a quality indicator, such as graded acceptability on sampled traffic, with an explicit objective beside latency and availability.
Run each task several times and report the chance that all attempts succeed. Single-run success overstates the consistency customers will experience.

records.t: LLM judges calibrated to human grades
records.x: Strong models can approximate human preference ratings, but show position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. Use them at scale only with a versioned human-graded sample to check agreement.

records.t: Cost and calls per completed task
records.x: Attribute token cost to each agent and workflow, and watch the distribution of model and tool calls per invocation to catch runaway loops before the invoice does.
Rates models by the length of task, in skilled human time, they complete half the time. Useful for scoping delegation; the measure is new and tied to software tasks.
Grading criteria drift as people review outputs, and LLM judges carry documented biases, including self-enhancement. Without a human-graded check, scores cannot be trusted to track quality.
Public agent benchmarks often have inadequate holdouts and ignore cost, and single runs hide inconsistency; models with equally strong test scores can behave differently in deployment.

records.t: NIST AI RMF and Generative AI Profile
records.x: A shared vocabulary for risk, legal and engineering: govern, map, measure and manage, with generative-AI risks such as confabulation. NIST has announced the framework is being revised.
Where the Act applies, classify each system against its risk tiers now: duties fall on deployers as well as providers, and obligations are phasing in.
Keep a short, standard record for every deployed model and dataset: intended use, how it was evaluated, known gaps and uses that are out of scope.
Give each agent its own identity, the narrowest permissions its task needs and logged activity, as for any insider with access to important systems.
Map each LLM risk, from prompt injection to unbounded consumption, to a named control or an accepted risk before launch. The agentic list is newer and still settling.
A certifiable management-system standard for AI, published 2023. Map existing controls to it first; certify where customers or regulators need independent assurance.
Assess how a system may affect people and society before building it and again at each material change, and feed the results into the risk register.
Keep permissions, logging and a tested shutdown path in the harness around the model, not in its instructions, so an authorised person can always pause it mid-task.
Disclose AI failures to those affected and share what failed, which controls broke and how to prevent it. The mechanisms for sharing across organisations are not yet established.

records.t: Human approval as the only safeguard
records.x: Automation erodes the skills and attention people need to supervise it and take over when it fails. Pair human review with controls and evidence that do not depend on it.

records.t: Shifting accountability to the model or provider
records.x: A tribunal held an airline liable for its chatbot's advice, and provider assurances do not transfer responsibility. Plan as though every AI output is the organisation's own statement.

records.t: Capturing prompts and outputs by default
records.x: The OpenTelemetry conventions make content capture opt-in and warn it is likely to contain personal data. Enable it only under a written policy with an owner, retention and access controls.

records.m: Rafael Gorski M. Souza and Paulo Cézar Stadzisz · 2016
records.x: Starts from named customer problems, not requested features, and derives customer needs and requirements from them. In an AI programme, every capability, including each agent, should then trace to a problem it solves. Confirm every requirement derives from a customer need, and each need from a named customer problem; cut the rest. MIT-licensed agent skill: github.com/RafaelGorski/Problem-Based-SRS.
records.h: Problem-Based Software Requirements Specification Rafael Gorski M. Souza and Paulo Cézar Stadzisz, Revista Eletrônica de Sistemas de Informação Framework

records.x: Its first rule is not to be afraid to launch without machine learning. That sets the right opening question for any sponsor: what simple baseline must the AI beat to justify its cost? Ship a heuristic or non-ML baseline first, instrument it, and require every model to beat it on the same metric.
records.h: Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering Martin Zinkevich, Google Guide

records.t: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
records.x: The ML code is a small fraction of a production ML system; the surrounding data, configuration and serving code carry most of the long-term cost. Budget for that, not for the demo. Inventory undeclared consumers, data dependencies and feedback loops around each model before committing to scale it.
records.h: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems D. Sculley et al., NeurIPS Paper

records.x: Separates predefined workflows from autonomous agents and argues for the simplest design that works. The publisher flags that the tooling described has since changed; read it for the design reasoning. For each proposed agent, document why a fixed workflow would not meet the requirement before granting it open-ended control.
records.h: Building effective agents Anthropic Guide

records.t: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
records.x: Measures capability as the length of task, in skilled human time, that a model completes half the time. A sober way to set scope: delegate work inside that horizon, not beyond it. Estimate how long your target tasks take a skilled person and compare that with the published time horizon of the model you plan to use.
records.h: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks Thomas Kwa et al., METR Paper

records.x: In interviews with 53 practitioners, 92% had met compounding data failures that surfaced late. The study ties them to practices that undervalue data work, which leaders can change. Log when each data issue was introduced and when it was detected; the gap is your cascade exposure.
records.h: "Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work": Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI Nithya Sambasivan et al., ACM CHI Paper

records.x: Introduces pass^k: the chance an agent succeeds on every one of k repeated attempts at the same task. A pilot that passes once is a demo; consistency is what customers experience. Run each evaluation task several times and report pass^k alongside the single-run success rate.
records.h: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains Shunyu Yao et al. Paper

records.x: Shows that agent evaluations often ignore cost and lack proper holdout sets, so headline accuracy can mislead. Ask for accuracy and cost together, measured on tasks the agent has not seen. Plot every candidate agent on cost versus accuracy, including simple baselines, and require results on a held-out task set.
records.h: AI Agents That Matter Sayash Kapoor et al. Paper

records.t: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
records.x: Strong models can approximate human preference ratings, which makes evaluation at scale affordable. The paper also documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases that must be controlled before trusting the scores. Swap answer order, vary length and use a different model family as judge; report agreement with a human-labelled sample.
records.h: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena Lianmin Zheng et al., NeurIPS Paper

records.x: Finds that people refine their evaluation criteria while grading outputs, so automated graders must be revisited as understanding grows. Evaluation is a managed asset, not a one-time setup. Version your grading criteria and LLM-judge prompts, and re-measure their agreement with human grades whenever criteria change.
records.h: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences Shreya Shankar et al. Paper

records.t: Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern…
records.x: Models with equally strong test scores can behave very differently in deployment. A strong pilot result does not, on its own, predict production behaviour. Evaluate candidate models on shifted and subgroup data that the pilot test set does not represent.
records.h: Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning Alexander D'Amour et al., JMLR Paper

records.m: UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs · living
records.x: An open-source evaluation framework co-developed by the UK AI Security Institute, covering coding, agentic and reasoning tasks. A shared, inspectable harness makes results reproducible and comparable across model vendors. Express pilot evaluations as versioned Inspect tasks so the same suite reruns unchanged on every model or prompt change.
records.h: Inspect UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs Framework

records.x: A standard set of questions about how a dataset was collected, labelled and intended to be used. Without those answers, no one can say whether pilot data represents production. Require a datasheet for every evaluation and fine-tuning dataset, including its collection process, known gaps and permitted uses.
records.h: Datasheets for Datasets Timnit Gebru et al., Communications of the ACM Paper

records.x: Shows how a system's structure of stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays drives its behaviour. AI systems that learn from their own outputs, or agents that call other agents, create exactly such loops. Draw the feedback loops the system creates, including outputs that return as inputs, and name the delay and the limit on each.
records.h: Thinking in Systems: A Primer Donella H. Meadows, edited by Diana Wright, Chelsea Green Publishing Book

records.x: A systematic method for developer testing: examples from the specification, then the code's structure, contracts and property-based tests. When coding agents write code faster than people can review it, tests must find what nobody tried. For each rule that money, permissions or limits depend on, write a property stating what must never happen and let a generator search for counterexamples.
records.h: Effective Software Testing: A developer's guide Maurício Aniche, Manning Book

records.x: Describes how Google turned launches into a repeatable discipline with a dedicated coordination role and a checklist. AI launches need the same rigour, plus questions specific to model behaviour. Extend the launch checklist with rows for evaluation results, abuse testing, rollback of model and prompt versions, and cost limits.
records.h: Reliable Product Launches at Scale Google, Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly) Book

records.x: Expose a change to a small share of traffic, compare it against a control, then widen. For models and prompts, whose failures are statistical rather than crashes, this comparison is an essential safety net. Route model and prompt changes through a canary with a control group and predefined quality, latency and cost thresholds.
records.h: Canarying Releases Google, The Site Reliability Workbook (O'Reilly) Book

records.x: Twenty-eight specific tests and monitoring needs drawn from a wide range of production ML systems. It turns 'is this ready for production?' into a score a review board can track. Score each system against the rubric at launch review and treat untested sections as open risks with named owners.
records.h: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction Eric Breck et al., IEEE Big Data Paper

records.x: The shared vocabulary security teams use for LLM application risk, from prompt injection to unbounded consumption. Asking which items a launch has mitigated is a fast, credible review question. Map each of the ten risks to a named control or an accepted-risk decision in the launch review record.
records.h: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 OWASP Gen AI Security Project Guide

records.t: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026
records.x: A peer-reviewed list of the most critical security risks for autonomous and agentic AI systems. Use it alongside the LLM Top 10 once a system can act, not just answer. Verify each agent runs with its own scoped identity and least-privilege tool permissions, never a shared human or service account.
records.h: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 OWASP Gen AI Security Project Guide

records.t: Guidelines for secure AI system development
records.x: Joint guidance from national cyber security agencies, organised by lifecycle: secure design, development, deployment, and operation and maintenance. A security baseline a board can point to. Confirm model weights, prompts and tool credentials are covered by the same asset inventory, access control and incident process as code.
records.h: Guidelines for secure AI system development UK NCSC, US CISA and international partners Guide

records.t: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
records.x: A model update shipped on positive evaluations and A/B results despite expert testers saying it felt off, then was rolled back. OpenAI committed to treating behaviour issues as launch-blocking. Give named expert reviewers authority to block a model release on qualitative findings, even when quantitative evaluations pass.
records.h: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy OpenAI Postmortem

records.x: Eighteen guidelines, validated with 49 design practitioners, for how AI features set expectations, handle mistakes and support correction. They shape how users experience the system on the days it is wrong. Review the launch UI against the guidelines on efficient correction, efficient dismissal and explaining why the system did what it did.
records.h: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction Saleema Amershi et al., Microsoft Research (ACM CHI) Paper

records.x: NIST's reference taxonomy of attacks on predictive and generative AI, including direct and indirect prompt injection and the security of agents. One vocabulary for security, engineering and risk teams. Use its attack categories as the headings of your AI threat model so findings map to a public reference.
records.h: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations NIST (NIST AI 100-2 E2025) Guide

records.x: An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Standardising on one protocol reduces bespoke integration work and gives security teams a single interface to review. Pin the protocol revision your servers support and review its authorization section before exposing any MCP server beyond localhost.
records.h: Model Context Protocol Specification (2026-07-28) Model Context Protocol project (LF Projects) Specification

records.x: An open protocol for agents built by different teams or vendors to discover each other and delegate tasks. It matters once agents multiply and must cooperate across organisational boundaries. Treat each Agent Card as an interface contract: version it, sign it, and review its declared skills and security schemes.
records.h: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification A2A Project, Linux Foundation Specification

records.m: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso · 2013
records.x: Brief latency spikes that are harmless in small systems come to dominate performance at scale. Agent workflows that chain many model and tool calls inherit this problem directly. Measure p99 latency per step and end to end for agent runs, and set per-call timeouts and hedging where steps are idempotent.
records.h: The Tail at Scale Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, Communications of the ACM Paper

records.x: Explains how overload in one component spreads through retries and dependencies until a whole service fails. Agents that retry automatically can turn a model-provider slowdown into exactly this. Cap retries with budgets and jittered backoff, propagate deadlines through agent steps, and load-test the provider-throttled case.
records.h: Addressing Cascading Failures Google, Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly) Book

records.x: Routing each query through a cascade, cheaper models first and stronger ones only when needed, matched the best single model at up to 98% lower cost. Model choice is a per-request decision. Log which model served each request and at what cost, then test whether a cheaper first-pass model meets the quality bar.
records.h: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou Paper

records.x: Vendor-neutral practice for allocating and controlling AI spend, including token-based pricing and scarce GPU capacity. AI costs move faster and reach more teams than typical cloud spend. Tag every model call with team, product and use case so cost per outcome can be reported, not just total spend.
records.h: FinOps for AI Overview FinOps Foundation Guide

records.t: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
records.x: A taxonomy of fourteen failure modes from expert-annotated traces, grouped into system design, misalignment between agents, and task verification. Adding agents adds coordination risk, not only capability. Classify failed multi-agent runs with the paper's taxonomy, and require an explicit verification step before any agent marks a task complete.
records.h: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? Mert Cemri et al. Paper

records.t: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
records.x: Proposes agent designs with provable resistance to prompt injection by limiting what an agent can do after reading untrusted input. Each trades some utility for security, a choice the business should own. For each agent, identify where untrusted content enters and which pattern, such as plan-then-execute, constrains actions after that point.
records.h: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections Luca Beurer-Kellner et al. Paper

records.t: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
records.x: Agents increasingly act on delegated credentials, and agent protocols such as MCP authorise through OAuth. This is the IETF's current security baseline for OAuth deployments. Confirm agent access tokens are audience-restricted and sender-constrained, and that public-client refresh tokens are rotated or sender-constrained.
records.h: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security IETF (RFC 9700) Standard

records.t: Semantic conventions for generative AI systems
records.x: The open standard for recording model calls, agent steps, tool use and token usage as telemetry. It keeps observability portable across vendors. Still marked Development, so expect changes. Emit gen_ai spans and token-usage metrics for every model and tool call, and record which convention version each service emits.
records.h: Semantic conventions for generative AI systems OpenTelemetry Specification

records.x: The web standard for carrying a trace identifier across services. When one user request passes through several agents, tools and vendors, it is what lets you reconstruct the whole path. Confirm traceparent headers propagate through every agent hop, tool call and third-party API, including asynchronous queues.
records.h: Trace Context W3C Standard

records.t: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure
records.x: Google's account of ubiquitous, low-overhead tracing across production services. Its lesson holds for agents: tracing pays off only when it is everywhere and cheap enough to leave on. Decide your trace sampling policy explicitly; keep full traces for errors, high-cost agent runs and sampled quality reviews.
records.h: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure Benjamin H. Sigelman et al., Google Paper

records.x: Defines reliability through indicators and objectives that reflect what users notice, and makes the target explicit. For AI systems, answer quality belongs beside latency and availability. Define at least one quality SLI per AI feature, such as graded answer acceptability on sampled traffic, with an explicit SLO target.
records.h: Service Level Objectives Google, Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly) Book

records.x: Blameless postmortems turn incidents into durable fixes and shared knowledge. AI incidents, such as harmful outputs or quality regressions, deserve the same written review as outages. Add AI-specific triggers to the postmortem policy: a quality regression, a harmful output reaching users, or an agent acting outside its scope.
records.h: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure Google, Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly) Book

records.t: A postmortem of three recent issues
records.x: Three infrastructure bugs intermittently degraded responses, and the evaluations in place did not capture what users were reporting. Quality can regress in production through infrastructure alone. Run quality evaluations continuously against true production endpoints, and keep a privacy-safe path to investigate user-reported bad outputs.
records.h: A postmortem of three recent issues Anthropic Postmortem

records.x: Treats measurement as reducing uncertainty for a decision, not reaching certainty, and uses the value of information to choose what to measure. It answers the claim that an AI system's benefits are intangible. For each production metric, name the decision it informs and estimate what better information is worth; retire metrics that inform no decision.
records.h: How to Measure Anything: Finding the Value of Intangibles in Business, 3rd Edition Douglas W. Hubbard, Wiley Book

records.x: Lean thinking for software. Its value stream map follows one request to delivery and shows where work waits, is handed off or is redone. When agents make coding faster, that waste is what remains. Map one change from request to release. Record working time, waiting time and where each defect was found, then remove the largest waste first.
records.h: Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit Mary Poppendieck and Tom Poppendieck, Addison-Wesley Book

records.m: European Parliament and Council of the European Union · 2024
records.x: EU law that tiers obligations by risk and places duties on deployers as well as providers. Obligations phase in over several years; establish which apply to your systems, and from when. Classify each AI system against Article 6 and Annex III, and confirm logging and human-oversight duties for any high-risk use.
records.h: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act) European Parliament and Council of the European Union Regulation

records.x: The certifiable management-system standard for AI, built on the same structure as ISO/IEC 27001. It gives boards an auditable answer to who owns AI risk, how it is assessed, and how it improves. Map existing AI controls to the standard's Annex A and record gaps before deciding whether to pursue certification.
records.h: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 Standard

records.x: Guidance on assessing how an AI system may affect individuals and society, and when in the lifecycle to do it. Done early, it shapes scope; done late, it becomes paperwork. Run the impact assessment before build and again at each material change, and link results to the risk register.
records.h: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 Information technology — Artificial intelligence (AI) — AI system impact assessment ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 Standard

records.x: A voluntary framework organised around four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. Useful as common language between risk, legal and engineering. NIST has announced it is being revised. Map each AI system's controls to the four functions and name an accountable owner for every gap.
records.h: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) NIST (NIST AI 100-1) Framework

records.x: Applies the AI RMF to generative AI, defining risks novel to or worsened by it, such as confabulation and value-chain integration, with suggested actions. A practical basis for governance reviews. Check the launch risk register covers each of the profile's risk categories, with an owner and a chosen action or explicit acceptance.
records.h: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile NIST (NIST AI 600-1) Framework

records.t: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
records.x: Defines the parties in an agent's lifecycle and proposes initial practices such as constraining actions, requiring approval, attributability and interruptibility. A starting map of who is accountable when an agent acts. For each production agent, confirm actions are attributable to a principal and that a tested shutdown path exists.
records.h: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems Yonadav Shavit et al., OpenAI Paper

records.t: Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era
records.x: Treats frontier models as insider risks: identity, limited privileges, logged activity and containment, enforced outside the model. A provider's assurances do not transfer responsibility; authority over intelligence stays with the deployer. Confirm access and action controls sit outside the model, every model action leaves tamper-proof evidence, and an authorised person can pause it mid-task.
records.h: Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era Satya Nadella, sn scratchpad Guide

records.x: A short, standard record of what a model is for, how it was evaluated, and where it should not be used. Write one before launch, not after an incident. Maintain a card for each deployed model or agent, including disaggregated evaluation results and explicitly out-of-scope uses.
records.h: Model Cards for Model Reporting Margaret Mitchell et al., FAT* 2019 Paper

records.m: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia · 2024
records.x: A tribunal held an airline liable for its website chatbot's incorrect advice, rejecting the idea that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. A small claim, but a clear signal. Ensure customer-facing AI answers on policy, price or entitlement are grounded in the authoritative source and logged for later review.
records.h: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia Postmortem

records.x: Automation erodes the skills and attention people need to supervise it and take over when it fails. Every 'human in the loop' promise for agents has to be designed against this. For each human approval step, measure approval rates and review time; near-total approval with seconds of review signals rubber-stamping.
records.h: Ironies of automation Lisanne Bainbridge, Automatica Paper

records.x: Is this worth building, and what would prove it?
Does it work on real data, measured honestly?
Can we ship it safely to real users?
Can it grow in users, agents and cost without losing control?
Can we see, fix and improve it in production?
Who is accountable, and can we prove it?
